q: Chemically, most enzymes are:
x: Most enzymes are globular proteins with a specific three-dimensional shape. Fibrous proteins such as keratin and collagen are structural, not catalytic.

q: Because an enzyme is a biological catalyst, at the end of the reaction it is:
o: Unchanged and can be used again
Used up as one of the reactants
Converted into one of the products
x: A catalyst speeds up a reaction without being used up. The enzyme comes out of the reaction unchanged and can act on more substrate.

q: Only a very small amount of an enzyme is needed in a cell because:
o: Enzymes raise the activation energy of reactions
Enzymes shift the reaction towards the products
The same enzyme molecule is used again and again
x: An enzyme is not used up, so one molecule can catalyse the conversion of many substrate molecules one after another. Enzymes lower, not raise, activation energy.

q: In a reversible reaction, an enzyme changes which of the following?
o: The final amount of product present at equilibrium
The speed at which equilibrium is reached
The energy released by the overall reaction
The chemical identity of the products
x: An enzyme only speeds up the approach to equilibrium. It does not change the equilibrium position, the overall energy change, or which products are formed.

q: The region of an enzyme where the substrate binds and is converted into products is called the:
x: The active site is the pocket or groove where the substrate binds and the reaction takes place. The allosteric site is a separate regulatory site.

q: The active site of an enzyme is formed by:
o: The entire polypeptide chain lying in a straight line
A small number of amino acids folded into a pocket or groove
The cofactor alone, without any amino acids
Nucleotides arranged in a fixed sequence
x: Only a few amino acids of the folded chain make up the active site, but the folding of the whole protein brings them together into a pocket or groove.

q: The active site has a binding site and a catalytic site. The function of the binding site is to:
o: Break or form bonds in the substrate
Hold the end product of the pathway
x: The binding site recognises the correct substrate and holds it. The catalytic site then carries out the chemical change.

q: Sucrase hydrolyses sucrose but has no action on lactose, although both are disaccharides. This property of enzymes is called:
x: Each enzyme acts only on its own substrate because only that substrate fits its active site. This is enzyme specificity.

q: The specificity of an enzyme is mainly due to:
o: The total size of the enzyme molecule
The amount of enzyme present in the cell
The shape and chemical nature of its active site
x: Only a substrate with a complementary shape and charge pattern can fit and bind in the active site. Size, amount and temperature do not decide which substrate is used.

q: A non-protein component that some enzymes need in order to be active is called a:
x: A cofactor is the non-protein part needed for activity. The apoenzyme is the protein part; a zymogen is an inactive precursor enzyme.

q: The protein part of a conjugated enzyme, without its cofactor, is called the:
x: The apoenzyme is the protein part alone and is inactive. The holoenzyme is the apoenzyme plus its cofactor.

q: A holoenzyme consists of:
x: A holoenzyme is the complete, active enzyme: the protein part (apoenzyme) joined with its non-protein cofactor.

q: An organic cofactor that is tightly (covalently) and permanently bound to its enzyme is called a:
x: A prosthetic group is an organic cofactor bound firmly to the enzyme. A coenzyme is organic but only loosely attached.

q: An organic cofactor that attaches loosely to the enzyme during the reaction and detaches afterwards is called a:
x: Coenzymes are organic molecules loosely attached to the enzyme, so they can separate after the reaction. Prosthetic groups stay tightly bound.

q: Inorganic metal ions such as Mg²⁺, Fe²⁺ and Zn²⁺ that are detachable cofactors of some enzymes are called:
x: Detachable inorganic ions that make an enzyme active are called activators. Coenzymes and prosthetic groups are organic.

q: Many coenzymes are made in the body from:
x: Vitamins, especially the B group, are the chief source of coenzymes. For example, NAD is made from niacin.

q: NAD⁺, which carries hydrogen in many reactions and is not permanently attached to its enzymes, is an example of a:
x: NAD⁺ is an organic, loosely attached cofactor, so it is a coenzyme. It is not inorganic, so it is not an activator ion.

q: An enzyme loses its activity when small ions are removed from its solution, and regains it fully when Mg²⁺ ions are added back. Here Mg²⁺ is acting as:
x: Mg²⁺ is an inorganic ion that can be removed and added back, so it is an activator. Prosthetic groups and coenzymes are organic molecules.

q: The haem group that is permanently and tightly bound to the protein of cytochromes is an example of a:
x: Haem is an organic, non-protein group firmly attached to the protein, which makes it a prosthetic group.

q: Enzymes that act in mitochondria and enzymes secreted into the gut are all synthesised on:
x: Enzymes are proteins, so they are made on ribosomes. The Golgi body packages secretory proteins but does not synthesise them.

q: Enzymes are very sensitive to changes in temperature and pH mainly because:
o: They are proteins whose three-dimensional shape is held by weak bonds
They are lipids that melt easily
They are carbohydrates that dissolve in acid
They contain DNA that breaks easily
x: An enzyme's shape, including its active site, is held by weak bonds such as hydrogen and ionic bonds, which heat and pH changes can disturb.

q: Which of the following is NOT an enzyme?
x: Insulin is a protein hormone, not a catalyst. Lipase, catalase and sucrase are enzymes; names ending in -ase usually indicate enzymes.

q: Pepsin is secreted in the stomach as inactive pepsinogen. Pepsinogen is converted to active pepsin by:
x: Some enzymes are secreted in an inactive form. Hydrochloric acid in the stomach converts pepsinogen into active pepsin.

q: The enzyme that breaks down hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen is:
x: Catalase decomposes harmful hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen. Amylase digests starch, lipase digests fats and pepsin digests proteins.

q: Compared with inorganic catalysts, a distinguishing feature of enzymes is that they:
o: Keep working faster as temperature rises without any limit
Are highly specific and work at mild body temperature and pH
Are used up in the reactions they catalyse
Act equally well on any substrate
x: Enzymes are specific and work under mild conditions. Above their optimum temperature they are denatured, and they are not used up.

q: The enzymes of the Krebs cycle are located in the:
x: Enzymes are often confined to particular parts of the cell. Krebs cycle enzymes are in the mitochondrial matrix.

q: Digestive enzymes such as pepsin are made inside cells but act outside them, in the gut. Such enzymes are called:
x: Enzymes that are secreted and act outside the cells that made them are extracellular. Intracellular enzymes act within the cell.

q: Urease acts only on urea, while lipase can hydrolyse many different fats. Which statement is correct?
o: Lipase acts on one substrate only, while urease acts on a range of related compounds
Urease and lipase can each act on all biological molecules
Urease acts on one substrate only, while lipase acts on a range of related fats
x: Urease shows absolute specificity for urea. Lipase shows a broader specificity for a group of related substrates, the fats.

q: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of enzymes?
o: They are specific in their action
They are destroyed after catalysing one reaction
Their activity is affected by pH
x: Enzymes are not destroyed by the reactions they catalyse; they are reused. Specificity, catalysis and pH sensitivity are all true characteristics.

q: The three-dimensional shape of an enzyme, including its active site, is ultimately determined by:
o: The number of cofactors it carries
The sequence of amino acids in its polypeptide chain
The cell organelle in which it is found
x: The amino acid sequence decides how the chain folds, and the folding produces the active site.

q: The coenzyme of a conjugated enzyme is completely removed. The protein that remains is:
o: An apoenzyme, and it is inactive
A holoenzyme, and it is fully active
A prosthetic group, and it is active
x: Without its cofactor the protein part is an apoenzyme, which cannot catalyse the reaction. Only the holoenzyme is active.

q: Which statement about enzymes as catalysts is correct?
o: They speed up reactions that are possible but too slow at body temperature
They make energetically impossible reactions happen
They supply the energy needed for the reaction
They are used up as the reaction proceeds
x: Enzymes speed up reactions that would occur anyway, only very slowly. They do not supply energy or make impossible reactions happen.

q: The minimum energy that reacting molecules must have before a reaction can start is called:
x: Activation energy is the energy barrier that must be crossed for reactants to react.

q: Enzymes speed up chemical reactions by:
o: Raising the temperature of the cell
x: Enzymes provide a pathway with a lower energy barrier, so more molecules can react at body temperature.

q: On an energy graph of the same reaction with and without an enzyme, the enzyme-catalysed reaction shows:
o: A lower final energy level of the products
A lower energy peak, with the same starting and final energy levels
The same energy peak with a lower starting level
x: An enzyme lowers only the activation energy barrier. The energy of the reactants and the products stays the same.

q: Which is the correct sequence of an enzyme-catalysed reaction?
x: Enzyme and substrate combine to form an enzyme–substrate complex, which then breaks up into product and free enzyme.

q: The lock-and-key model of enzyme action was proposed by:
x: Emil Fischer proposed the lock-and-key model. Koshland later proposed the induced-fit model.

q: The induced-fit model of enzyme action was proposed by:
x: Koshland proposed that the active site changes shape when the substrate binds, which is the induced-fit model.

q: According to the lock-and-key model, the active site of an enzyme:
o: Is flexible and moulds itself around the substrate
Changes its shape permanently after each reaction
Is rigid, with a fixed shape complementary to the substrate
Is formed only after the substrate has bound
x: In the lock-and-key model, the active site is a rigid structure into which only the exactly matching substrate fits.

q: According to the induced-fit model:
o: The active site is rigid and never changes shape
The active site changes shape on binding the substrate to fit it more closely
The substrate permanently changes the enzyme's structure
The enzyme is denatured each time it binds a substrate
x: In induced fit, the active site is flexible; substrate binding causes it to mould around the substrate. It returns to its original shape afterwards.

q: Some enzymes can act on several structurally related substrates. This observation is better explained by:
o: The lock-and-key model, because the active site is rigid
Feedback inhibition, because the end product controls the enzyme
Denaturation, because the active site loses its shape
The induced-fit model, because the active site is flexible
x: A flexible active site can adjust to related substrates of slightly different shape. A rigid lock would accept only one exact key.

q: After the products are released, the active site of the enzyme:
o: Is permanently altered and cannot be reused
Stays bound to the products forever
Is destroyed along with the substrate
Is free and in its original form, ready for another substrate
x: The enzyme is unchanged at the end, so its active site can accept another substrate molecule.

q: In the enzyme–substrate complex, the substrate is held in the active site mainly by:
o: Weak, temporary bonds such as hydrogen and ionic bonds
x: The substrate is held by weak bonds so that it can be released easily after the reaction. Peptide and glycosidic bonds are strong covalent bonds within molecules.

q: One way in which an enzyme lowers activation energy is by:
o: Heating the substrate molecules in the active site
Holding substrates so that their bonds are strained or their reacting groups are brought together
Adding the energy of ATP to every reaction
Increasing the temperature of the cytoplasm
x: In the active site, substrates are held in the right orientation and their bonds are put under strain, so less energy is needed to react.

q: When an enzyme meets its substrate, the first thing formed is:
x: The substrate first binds to the active site to form an enzyme–substrate complex, which then changes into products.

q: A reaction is catalysed by an enzyme. Compared with the uncatalysed reaction, which statement is correct?
o: The activation energy and the energy of the products both decrease
Only the energy of the products decreases
The activation energy increases, so the reaction speeds up
x: An enzyme lowers the energy barrier but does not change the energy of the reactants or products.

q: A substrate binds to the active site of its enzyme because:
o: It is the same size as the whole enzyme
Its shape and chemical charges are complementary to the active site
It is covalently fixed there by a prosthetic group
x: Binding depends on a complementary fit of shape and charges between the substrate and the active site.

q: In the lock-and-key model, the 'key' represents the:
x: The substrate is the key that fits into the enzyme's active site, which is the lock.

q: Glucose burns in air only when strongly heated, yet in cells it is oxidised at 37 °C. This is mainly because:
o: Cells are much hotter than the surroundings
Enzymes lower the activation energy of each step
Cells contain far more oxygen than air
x: Enzymes lower the activation energy, so the reactions of respiration can proceed at body temperature.

q: Studies show that an enzyme's active site closes around its substrate only after the substrate binds. This supports the:
x: A change in shape of the active site on binding is the central idea of the induced-fit model. The lock-and-key model assumes a rigid site.

q: Which statement about the enzyme–substrate complex is correct?
o: It is short-lived and breaks up to release the products and the free enzyme
It is a permanent compound that is stored in the cell
It is the final product of the reaction
It forms only when an inhibitor is present
x: The ES complex is a temporary intermediate. It quickly gives products and the enzyme is set free.

q: Maltase binds maltose at its active site and, after the reaction, releases:
x: Maltase hydrolyses maltose into two glucose molecules. Sucrose gives glucose and fructose; lactose gives glucose and galactose.

q: Which statement about enzyme-catalysed reactions is correct?
o: An enzyme may join two substrates into one product or split one substrate into two
Each enzyme makes many different products from one substrate
x: Enzymes catalyse both building-up and breaking-down reactions, depending on the enzyme.

q: Salivary amylase cannot digest proteins because:
o: Amylase is denatured by contact with proteins
Proteins have an activation energy no enzyme can lower
Proteins do not fit the shape and chemistry of its active site
Amylase works only in the stomach
x: Amylase's active site fits starch, not proteins. Amylase acts in the mouth, not the stomach.

q: When an enzyme lowers the activation energy of a reaction at a fixed temperature, the reaction speeds up because:
o: The temperature of the solution rises
A larger proportion of molecules now have enough energy to react
The products have more energy than before
x: Temperature, and so the speed of the molecules, has not changed. With a lower barrier, more of the molecules already present have enough energy to react.

q: After the substrate is held at the binding site, the part of the active site that actually converts it into products is the:
x: The active site has a binding site, which holds the substrate, and a catalytic site, which carries out the chemical change.

q: In reactions catalysed by dehydrogenase enzymes, the coenzyme NAD⁺ helps by:
o: Forming the active site of every enzyme
Accepting hydrogen removed from the substrate
x: Dehydrogenases remove hydrogen from their substrates, and NAD⁺ accepts it, becoming NADH.

q: The comparison of a hand fitting into a glove, which changes shape around the hand, describes which model?
x: The glove, like a flexible active site, changes shape to fit the hand, which is the induced-fit idea.

q: Which statement is NOT true of the induced-fit model?
o: Binding of the substrate changes the shape of the active site
The active site fits the substrate closely after binding
The active site has a fixed, rigid shape before and after binding
x: A rigid active site is the lock-and-key idea. In induced fit the active site is flexible and changes shape on binding.

q: Which is the correct order of events in enzyme action according to the induced-fit model?
o: Active site changes shape → substrate binds → products are released → bonds are strained
Products are released → substrate binds → bonds are strained → active site changes shape
Bonds are strained → substrate binds → products are released → active site changes shape
Substrate binds → active site changes shape → bonds are strained → products are released
x: The substrate binds first, which induces the change in the active site; the close fit strains bonds; then the products leave.

q: A mutation changes one amino acid in the active site of an enzyme so that its charge is altered. The most likely result is that:
o: The enzyme becomes active on all substrates
The substrate binds poorly, so the reaction slows or stops
The enzyme's optimum temperature becomes higher
The products of the reaction are changed into new molecules
x: Binding depends on complementary shape and charge. Altering an active-site amino acid weakens substrate binding and catalysis.

q: Hydrogen peroxide breaks down slowly on its own, but rapidly when catalase is added. With catalase, the products are:
o: Water and hydrogen, different from without the enzyme
Water and oxygen, the same as without the enzyme
Only oxygen, since the enzyme keeps the water
x: An enzyme changes only the rate. Hydrogen peroxide always gives water and oxygen.

q: Cells use enzymes, instead of high temperatures, to speed up their reactions mainly because:
o: High temperatures slow down all chemical reactions
High temperatures would damage cell proteins and are not specific
Enzymes raise the activation energy of reactions
Cells have no way to remove heat
x: Heat speeds reactions without control and would denature proteins. Enzymes lower activation energy specifically at body temperature.

q: Products leave the active site after the reaction mainly because:
o: They are pushed out by the inhibitor
The enzyme is denatured after each reaction
They no longer fit the active site as well as the substrate did
They are covalently bonded to the enzyme
x: Products have a different shape from the substrate, so they no longer fit well and are released.

q: The temperature at which an enzyme works at its fastest rate is called its:
x: Each enzyme works fastest at its optimum temperature. Above it, the enzyme starts to denature.

q: The optimum temperature of most human enzymes is about:
x: Most human enzymes work best near normal body temperature, about 37 °C.

q: When the temperature of an enzyme reaction is raised from 10 °C to 30 °C, the rate increases because:
o: Molecules move faster, so enzyme and substrate collide more often
x: Below the optimum, a rise in temperature gives molecules more kinetic energy and more collisions between enzyme and substrate.

q: Above the optimum temperature, the rate of an enzyme reaction falls because:
o: The enzyme is denatured and its active site loses its shape
x: High temperature breaks the weak bonds holding the enzyme's shape, so the active site no longer fits the substrate.

q: When an enzyme is denatured by heat, the bonds that are broken are mainly:
o: Hydrogen and ionic bonds holding its three-dimensional shape
x: Heat breaks the weak bonds that maintain the folded shape. Peptide bonds of the primary structure are not broken by ordinary heating.

q: An enzyme shows almost no activity at 0 °C, but when warmed to 37 °C it works normally. This shows that:
o: Low temperature denatures the enzyme permanently
Low temperature inactivates the enzyme temporarily without denaturing it
x: At low temperature molecules move slowly, so activity is very low, but the shape is not destroyed. Activity returns on warming.

q: An enzyme solution is boiled and then cooled back to its optimum temperature. The enzyme will:
o: Remain inactive, because heat denaturation is permanent
x: Boiling denatures the enzyme. Its active site does not regain its shape on cooling, so it stays inactive.

q: The optimum pH of pepsin is about:
x: Pepsin works in the strongly acidic stomach and has an optimum pH of about 2.

q: The optimum pH of salivary amylase is about:
x: Salivary amylase works in the mouth, where conditions are close to neutral; its optimum pH is about 6.8.

q: Pancreatic lipase works best in a medium that is:
x: Pancreatic lipase acts in the small intestine, where pancreatic juice and bile make the contents alkaline; its optimum is about pH 8–9. Strongly acidic conditions suit pepsin in the stomach instead.

q: Which enzyme is correctly matched with its approximate optimum pH?
x: Catalase works best near pH 7.6. Pepsin's optimum is about 2, salivary amylase's about 6.8 and pancreatic lipase's about 9.

q: Trypsin, a protein-digesting enzyme from the pancreas, works best in:
o: Strongly acidic conditions, as in the stomach
Slightly alkaline conditions, as in the small intestine
Weakly acidic conditions, at about pH 4.5
Very strongly alkaline conditions, at about pH 12
x: Trypsin acts in the small intestine, where pancreatic juice makes the medium slightly alkaline, around pH 8.

q: Pepsin is placed in a solution at pH 8. Its activity:
o: Falls sharply, because the pH is far from its optimum
Increases, because alkaline pH suits all proteases
Stays the same, because pH does not affect pepsin
Increases, because pepsin is converted to trypsin
x: Pepsin works best near pH 2. At pH 8 the charges on its active site change and it becomes inactive.

q: A change in pH affects enzyme activity mainly because it:
o: Changes the temperature of the solution
Breaks the peptide bonds of the enzyme
Adds water molecules to the substrate
Changes the charges on amino acids, especially at the active site
x: pH alters the ionisation of acidic and basic groups. This changes the shape and charge of the active site, so substrate binding is affected.

q: Which statement about pH and enzymes is correct?
o: All enzymes have an optimum pH of 7
All enzymes work best in acidic conditions
pH has no effect on enzyme activity
Each enzyme has its own optimum pH, and different enzymes have different optima
x: Optimum pH varies: about 2 for pepsin, 6.8 for salivary amylase and 9 for pancreatic lipase.

q: Substrate is present in excess. If the enzyme concentration is doubled, the rate of reaction:
x: With plenty of substrate, rate depends on how many enzyme molecules are present, so doubling the enzyme roughly doubles the rate.

q: With substrate in excess, increasing the enzyme concentration increases the rate because:
o: More active sites are available to bind substrate
x: More enzyme molecules mean more active sites, so more substrate molecules can be converted per unit time.

q: Enzyme concentration is increased step by step while the amount of substrate is kept small and fixed. The rate eventually stops increasing because:
o: The extra enzyme inhibits the reaction
x: Once there are far more active sites than substrate molecules, adding enzyme cannot increase the rate; the shortage of substrate limits it.

q: Enzyme concentration is kept constant while substrate concentration is increased. The rate of reaction:
o: Increases at first and then levels off
x: Rate rises as more substrate binds, then levels off when all active sites are occupied.

q: At high substrate concentration the rate of an enzyme reaction stops rising because:
o: All the active sites are occupied
The enzyme is denatured by the substrate
The products raise the activation energy
x: When every active site is in use, the enzyme is saturated, and extra substrate must wait its turn.

q: An enzyme reaction is already at its maximum rate because the enzyme is saturated with substrate. Which change would increase the rate further?
o: Lowering the temperature below the optimum
x: At saturation every active site is busy, so only more active sites (more enzyme) can raise the rate. More substrate has no effect.

q: At very low substrate concentration, with plenty of enzyme, the rate of an enzyme reaction is limited mainly by:
o: The number of substrate molecules available
The number of enzyme molecules available
The pH of the solution only
x: With many free active sites, rate depends on how often substrate molecules reach them, so substrate is limiting.

q: A graph of rate of an enzyme reaction against temperature typically shows that the rate:
o: Rises in a straight line at all temperatures
Rises gradually to a peak and then falls steeply
Falls at first and then rises
x: Rate rises with temperature up to the optimum, then drops quickly as the enzyme is denatured.

q: A graph of the activity of one enzyme against pH typically shows:
o: A peak at the optimum pH, with lower activity on either side
A straight line rising with pH
Constant activity at all pH values
Lowest activity at the optimum pH
x: Activity is highest at the optimum pH and falls as pH moves either above or below it.

q: A very high body temperature, well above 37 °C, is dangerous partly because:
o: Body enzymes begin to lose their shape and stop working
Enzymes start working at an unlimited rate
Activation energies of reactions rise sharply
x: Above their optimum, enzymes begin to denature, so their active sites lose shape and metabolic reactions slow down.

q: Salivary amylase stops digesting starch once food reaches the stomach mainly because:
o: The stomach is too cold for the enzyme
Bile in the stomach coats the starch
The stomach's acidity is far from its optimum pH
x: Salivary amylase works best near pH 6.8. The strongly acidic stomach contents inactivate it.

q: Keeping food in a refrigerator slows its spoilage mainly because:
o: Enzymes of microbes work very slowly at low temperature
Low temperature denatures all microbial enzymes
Cold increases the activation energy of all reactions
Cold destroys all the substrates in food
x: At low temperature enzyme reactions are slow, so microbial growth and decay slow down. The enzymes are not destroyed.

q: Which feature of an enzyme is NOT changed when it is denatured by heat?
x: Heat breaks the weak bonds of the folded shape, but not the peptide bonds, so the amino acid sequence stays the same.

q: An amino acid in an enzyme's active site must carry a negative charge to bind the substrate. If the pH is lowered strongly, the most likely effect is that:
o: The charge becomes more negative, so binding improves
Added H⁺ ions neutralise this charge, so substrate binding falls
The enzyme's peptide bonds join more strongly
The optimum temperature of the enzyme rises
x: At low pH, extra H⁺ ions are taken up by negatively charged groups, removing the charge needed to hold the substrate.

q: The loss of an enzyme's three-dimensional shape caused by high temperature or extreme pH is called:
x: Denaturation is the loss of the folded shape, and with it the active site, caused by heat or extreme pH.

q: Stomach contents entering the duodenum are neutralised by alkaline pancreatic juice and bile. This is necessary because:
o: Pancreatic enzymes need strongly acidic conditions
Alkali raises body temperature for enzymes
Pancreatic enzymes need slightly alkaline conditions
Acid would convert pancreatic enzymes into pepsin
x: Pancreatic enzymes such as trypsin and lipase have alkaline optimum pH values, so the acid from the stomach must be neutralised.

q: A substance that reduces or stops the activity of an enzyme is called:
x: An inhibitor lowers enzyme activity. An activator or coenzyme helps the enzyme work.

q: A competitive inhibitor works by:
o: Binding to a site away from the active site
Resembling the substrate and binding to the active site
x: A competitive inhibitor has a shape similar to the substrate, so it competes for and occupies the active site.

q: The effect of a competitive inhibitor can be reduced by:
x: With more substrate, substrate molecules win the competition for the active site more often.

q: A non-competitive inhibitor binds to:
o: The active site, in place of the substrate
The substrate, before it reaches the enzyme
A site other than the active site, changing the active site's shape
The product, after it leaves the enzyme
x: A non-competitive inhibitor attaches elsewhere on the enzyme, and this distorts the active site so the reaction cannot proceed normally.

q: Adding more substrate does not overcome non-competitive inhibition because:
o: The inhibitor does not compete for the active site but alters the enzyme's shape
The substrate is destroyed by the inhibitor
The inhibitor is more concentrated than the enzyme
The substrate binds to the inhibitor instead
x: Since the inhibitor binds elsewhere, extra substrate cannot push it off; the inhibited enzymes remain inactive.

q: Irreversible inhibitors inactivate enzymes by:
o: Binding loosely and leaving when substrate increases
Speeding up the formation of products
Binding very tightly, often by covalent bonds, so the enzyme is permanently inactivated
x: Irreversible inhibitors form strong bonds with the enzyme, usually at the active site, so the enzyme cannot recover.

q: Cyanide is a deadly poison mainly because it:
o: Acts as a competitive inhibitor of salivary amylase
Breaks the peptide bonds of all proteins
Raises body temperature until enzymes boil
Inhibits a key enzyme of cellular respiration, blocking ATP production
x: Cyanide inhibits cytochrome oxidase of the respiratory chain, so cells cannot use oxygen to make ATP.

q: Malonate has a structure very similar to succinate and binds to the active site of succinate dehydrogenase, slowing the reaction. Malonate is:
x: Malonate resembles succinate and occupies the same active site, which is the mark of competitive inhibition.

q: In feedback inhibition:
o: The substrate inhibits the last enzyme of the pathway
A poison permanently destroys the first enzyme
Heat stops all the enzymes of a pathway
The end product of a pathway inhibits an enzyme early in that pathway
x: In feedback inhibition, the final product of a pathway switches off an earlier, usually the first, enzyme.

q: The main advantage of feedback inhibition to a cell is that it:
o: Increases the amount of end product without limit
Speeds up the denaturation of enzymes
Prevents excess production and wastage of the end product
x: When enough end product is present, the pathway slows down, so the cell does not waste resources making more.

q: In a pathway W → X → Y → Z, the end product Z builds up and inhibits the enzyme that converts W to X. As a result:
o: Less X, Y and Z are made until the level of Z falls
The enzyme converting Y to Z is destroyed
W is converted directly into Z
x: Blocking the first step reduces the supply to all later steps. When Z is used up, the first enzyme works again.

q: In feedback inhibition, the end product usually binds to the first enzyme of the pathway at:
o: Its active site, in place of the substrate
x: The end product usually differs from the first substrate and binds at an allosteric site, changing the active site's shape.

q: Which statement about competitive inhibition is correct?
o: The inhibitor binds only at the allosteric site
The inhibitor permanently destroys the enzyme
The inhibitor is converted into product as fast as the substrate
The inhibitor and the substrate cannot both be bound to the active site at the same time
x: The two molecules compete for the same active site, so only one can occupy it at a time.

q: An inhibitor greatly reduces the rate of a reaction at low substrate concentration, but at very high substrate concentration the rate is almost normal. The inhibitor is most likely:
x: Only a competitive inhibitor can be outcompeted by large amounts of substrate.

q: An inhibitor reduces the rate of an enzyme reaction by the same proportion at all substrate concentrations, and adding more substrate never restores the normal rate. The inhibitor is most likely:
x: A non-competitive inhibitor acts away from the active site, so extra substrate cannot reverse its effect.

q: Reversible and irreversible inhibitors differ in that:
o: Reversible inhibitors bind strongly and permanently, while irreversible ones detach easily
Reversible inhibitors are always proteins, while irreversible ones are always vitamins
Reversible inhibitors raise enzyme activity, while irreversible ones lower it
Reversible inhibitors bind by weak bonds and can detach, while irreversible ones bind strongly and permanently
x: Reversible inhibitors are held by weak bonds and can come off; irreversible inhibitors form strong, often covalent, bonds.

q: A site on an enzyme, other than the active site, where regulatory molecules can bind and change the enzyme's activity is called the:
x: Allosteric means 'other site'. Molecules binding there change the shape of the active site.

q: Which type of inhibitor permanently reduces the number of working enzyme molecules, so its effect lasts until new enzyme is made?
x: An irreversible inhibitor destroys the activity of the enzyme it binds, so only newly made enzyme can restore activity.

q: The control of a metabolic pathway in which its own end product inhibits an earlier enzyme is called:
x: This self-regulating control is feedback inhibition.

q: Which statement is NOT true of competitive inhibitors?
o: They bind to the allosteric site of the enzyme
They resemble the substrate in shape
They bind to the active site
Their effect is reduced by adding more substrate
x: Competitive inhibitors bind to the active site, not to an allosteric site. The other statements are true of them.

q: A solution of enzyme plus inhibitor is dialysed to remove all small molecules, and the enzyme's activity returns to normal. The inhibitor was:
x: Removing the inhibitor restored activity, so it was bound by weak bonds. An irreversible inhibitor would remain attached.

q: When the level of the end product of a feedback-controlled pathway falls, the first enzyme:
o: Becomes active again as the end product detaches
Is destroyed and must be replaced
x: Feedback inhibition is reversible: as end product is used up, it leaves the enzyme and the pathway restarts.

q: Which pairing correctly matches the inhibitor type with the place it binds?
o: Competitive – a site other than the active site; non-competitive – active site
Competitive – the substrate; non-competitive – the product
Competitive – the cofactor; non-competitive – the substrate
Competitive – active site; non-competitive – a site other than the active site
x: Competitive inhibitors occupy the active site, while non-competitive inhibitors bind elsewhere on the enzyme.

q: When an inhibitor binds to an enzyme, the structure formed is called the:
x: Enzyme plus inhibitor forms an enzyme–inhibitor (EI) complex, which cannot form products.

q: Unlike heat denaturation, a reversible inhibitor:
o: Breaks the weak bonds that hold the enzyme's shape
Lowers enzyme activity without permanently destroying the enzyme's structure
Changes the amino acid sequence of the enzyme
x: A reversible inhibitor can leave the enzyme, which then works normally. Denaturation permanently destroys the enzyme's shape.

q: The degree of inhibition caused by a competitive inhibitor depends on:
o: The concentration of the product alone
The relative concentrations of inhibitor and substrate
Whether the enzyme has an allosteric site
x: Substrate and inhibitor compete for the same site, so whichever is more plentiful occupies more active sites.

q: Mg²⁺ increases the activity of some enzymes, while cyanide decreases the activity of a respiratory enzyme. Mg²⁺ and cyanide act respectively as:
o: A prosthetic group and a coenzyme
x: Mg²⁺ is an inorganic activator. Cyanide is an enzyme inhibitor.

q: Which statement is NOT a feature of feedback inhibition?
o: The end product binds permanently and destroys the first enzyme
It controls the rate of a metabolic pathway
It prevents excess end product from building up
The inhibiting molecule is the pathway's own end product
x: Feedback inhibition is reversible; the end product does not destroy the enzyme. The other statements describe it correctly.

q: An enzyme solution is treated with a small amount of irreversible inhibitor, which becomes fully bound to some enzyme molecules. If more enzyme is then added, the rate:
o: Stays the same, because the inhibitor blocks all enzymes
Increases, because the newly added enzyme molecules are not inhibited
Falls, because the inhibitor is released
Falls to zero, because the new enzyme is denatured
x: All the inhibitor is already bound, so the extra enzyme molecules have free active sites and add to the rate.

q: An inhibitor fits into the active site like a wrong key that fits a lock but cannot turn it. This describes:
x: A molecule that occupies the active site without being converted is a competitive inhibitor.

q: Compared with the substrate, a non-competitive inhibitor usually:
o: Has exactly the same shape as the substrate
Does not resemble the substrate in shape
Is converted into the same product
Binds to the active site in place of the substrate
x: A non-competitive inhibitor binds at another site, so it does not need to look like the substrate.
